title: How to Land on a Government Watch List
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the U.S. government terrorist watch list, its origins in Homeland Security Presidential Directive 6 (May 2003) and the consolidation after 9/11, and how it differs from the no fly and selectee lists. They cover the Terrorist Screening Center (an FBI branch), the TRIP redress process, the disputed size of the list (ACLU's million-plus versus TSA's under 400,000), notable false positives such as Sen. John Lewis, Sister Glenn McPhee, and an eight-year-old boy, the 2009 narrowing of criteria, and the Treasury's SDN list. They also discuss ways people might get flagged (last-minute flights, cash purchases, search terms), state-level profiling criteria, and the Patriot Act postal spying proposal that was dropped. The episode closes with listener mail from a twin sister in Hawaii.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about deadlines and relief, then introduce the topic of the government watch list and its critics.

segments.title: Origins of the consolidated terrorist watch list
segments.summary: The hosts discuss pre-9/11 intelligence failures and turf wars between agencies, then HSPD-6 in 2003 that created a consolidated terrorist watch list.

segments.title: Criteria and size of the list
segments.summary: The 2009 revised criteria require more than a single source and mere association is insufficient. Estimates of list size differ: ACLU says a million or more, TSA says under 400,000.

segments.title: Nominations, Terrorist Screening Center, and the no fly list
segments.summary: Any government agency could nominate a person, who is then reviewed and passed to the Terrorist Screening Center, an FBI branch. The no fly list and selectee list are distinct from the broader watch list.

segments.title: False positives and wrongful listings
segments.summary: Cases include Rep. John Lewis, Sister Glenn McPhee, an eight-year-old boy, a Stanford doctoral candidate, and Army veterans stranded abroad. Redress can take a long time.

segments.title: How people get on the list and ways to be flagged
segments.summary: Examples include membership in extremist groups like ELF, along with patterns such as last-minute or cash purchases, and Google searches. State-level criteria can flag people, and the Patriot Act postal spying idea was dropped. The Privacy Act exemption and the Constitutional concerns are raised.

segments.title: Checking your status and the Treasury SDN list
segments.summary: Being stopped at airports or detained is one sign of being listed. Redress numbers are used to clear travel. The Treasury's Specially Designated Nationals list is a separate list tied to freezing business dealings.

segments.title: Sponsor and closing plug
segments.summary: Plugs for the website search and social media, plus a promo for the video podcast Stuff from the Future.

segments.title: Listener mail from a twin sister
segments.summary: A listener writes about her twin sister, a Marine's wife in Hawaii, and how the show helps them feel close. The hosts respond with thanks.
